issues.subcategory: incorrect serial mediation computation
issues.description: Hypothesis 4 is a serial mediation model from experienced incivility to negative emotions to compassion fatigue to enacted incivility. The indirect effect should be the product of three paths (experienced incivility → negative emotions, negative emotions → compassion fatigue, compassion fatigue → enacted incivility), often a × d × b or equivalent. The manuscript states that the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying only the first and last stages and labels this as “a × d,” which is also the same notation used for the two-path indirect effect in Hypothesis 2. This is mathematically inconsistent with a serial mediation model and makes the reported indirect effect uninterpretable or likely incorrect.
issues.quote: Here, the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying the first and last stages in the serial mediation process (a × d).

issues.subcategory: indirect-effect values inconsistent with reported path coefficients
issues.description: The reported serial indirect effect for Hypothesis 4 is inconsistent with the regression coefficients in Table 2. Table 2 reports T2 customer incivility → T3 negative emotions B = .26, T3 negative emotions → T4 compassion fatigue B = .37, and T4 compassion fatigue → T4 enacted incivility B = .57. The product is approximately .055, matching the reported B = .06 only if all three paths are multiplied. But the results text says only first and last stages were multiplied. In addition, the results section gives SE = .04 for this indirect effect, whereas Table 2 gives SE = .02. These inconsistencies raise concern about analytic/reporting accuracy.
issues.quote: As expected, Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients (B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]).

issues.subcategory: p value inconsistent with confidence interval
issues.description: For the Hypothesis 4 indirect effect, the reported estimate and standard error in the text imply a z/t statistic of about 1.5 (.06/.04), which would not yield p < .01. The confidence interval [0.02, 0.10] and Table 2 SE = .02 imply significance, but the text-reported SE = .04 does not. This is an internal statistical inconsistency that prevents evaluation of the claim.
issues.quote: Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients (B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]).

issues.subcategory: incorrect CFA reporting
issues.description: The confirmatory factor analysis fit statistic is missing the test-statistic label. The text reports only “(269) = 862.05,” presumably omitting χ². This impairs interpretability and suggests incomplete or careless reporting of a core measurement validity analysis.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99) and fit the data better than alternative models with fewer factors.

issues.subcategory: alternative CFA models not reported
issues.description: The manuscript states that the hypothesized factor model fit better than alternative models but does not report the alternative models tested, their fit indices, chi-square difference tests or other comparison statistics, factor loadings, or correlations among latent factors. Given the extremely high observed correlations among constructs, discriminant validity is a central concern, and the absence of full CFA results prevents evaluation.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99) and fit the data better than alternative models with fewer factors.

issues.subcategory: poor discriminant validity among constructs
issues.description: The reported correlations among key variables are extremely high, including T4 compassion fatigue with T4 enacted incivility r = .94, T3 negative emotions with T4 enacted incivility r = .87, T2 customer incivility with T4 compassion fatigue r = .85, and T3 negative emotions with T4 compassion fatigue r = .86. Such correlations raise serious concerns that constructs are not empirically distinct, may reflect common method/negative response bias, or may be artifacts of overlapping item valence and self-report. This undermines mediation interpretations and claims that separate affective, fatigue, and behavioral constructs are being modeled.

issues.subcategory: implausibly high R-squared values suggest overfitting or construct redundancy
issues.description: The model reports R² = .81 for enacted incivility and very high correlations among predictors and outcome. This may indicate substantial construct redundancy, common method variance, or same-time measurement artifacts, especially because T4 compassion fatigue and T4 enacted incivility are measured concurrently. The manuscript interprets these as substantive longitudinal effects without sufficiently addressing the possibility that measurement overlap or response style drives results.

issues.subcategory: same-source self-report of predictor, mediator, and outcome
issues.description: All substantive variables, including enacted incivility toward patients, were measured by nurses’ self-reports. Self-report of socially undesirable behavior such as patient-directed incivility is vulnerable to social desirability, underreporting, mood-congruent reporting, and common method bias. Temporal separation alone does not eliminate these problems, especially with high correlations and concurrent mediator-outcome measurement at T4.
issues.quote: This study has several limitations that should be discussed. First, our data were collected using self-report questionnaires.

issues.subcategory: concurrent measurement of mediator and outcome
issues.description: Compassion fatigue and enacted incivility are both measured at Time 4 in the hypothesized serial mediation. This prevents establishing temporal ordering between compassion fatigue and enacted incivility and weakens the mediation claim that compassion fatigue leads to later enacted incivility. The study is described as longitudinal and temporally separated, but the final mediator and outcome are contemporaneous.
issues.quote: T4 Compassion Fatigue | 2.73 | 1.22 ... T4 Enacted Incivility | 2.77 | 1.21

issues.subcategory: overstated causal inference from observational panel data
issues.description: The manuscript claims that the longitudinal mediation model allows stronger causal inferences and that repeated exposure “leads to” outcomes, but the design is observational, non-randomized, self-report, and does not adequately rule out stable individual differences, reverse causation, shared negative affectivity, workload, unit climate, staffing, shift type, or other confounds. Temporal ordering alone is insufficient for causal mediation.
issues.quote: This method also supports a lower likelihood of third variable effects ... and allows for stronger causal inferences by modeling the longitudinal effects of predictors across multiple points in time.

issues.subcategory: causal language unsupported
issues.description: The abstract and discussion use causal phrasing such as “leads to,” “impact,” “drives,” and “downstream costs.” Given correlational observational data, substantial common-method concerns, and incomplete temporal separation, such statements overstate what can be concluded.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility.

issues.subcategory: lack of autoregressive controls for focal outcomes
issues.description: Although Time 1 controls are mentioned, the presented mediation regressions do not clearly control for prior levels of the mediator and outcome variables corresponding to each later variable (e.g., T1/T2 negative emotions predicting T3 negative emotions, T1/T3 compassion fatigue predicting T4 compassion fatigue, prior enacted incivility predicting T4 enacted incivility). Without autoregressive controls, paths may reflect stable between-person differences rather than within-person change over time. This is particularly problematic because baseline correlations are very high.
issues.quote: Table 2 | Simultaneous mediation regression results ... T2 Customer Incivility ... T3 Negative Emotions ... T4 Compassion Fatigue ... T4 Enacted Incivility

issues.subcategory: unclear control-variable strategy
issues.description: The manuscript refers to Time 1 controls and Table 1 is titled “with Time 1 Controls,” but Table 2 includes only work hours as controls and does not show Time 1 values of the focal constructs as covariates. It is unclear which controls were included in each model, why they were selected, and whether results depend on them. This lack of transparency impairs replication and interpretation.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents intercorrelations among study variables and descriptive information.

issues.subcategory: sample size inconsistencies
issues.description: The manuscript reports a final sample of N = 372 after exclusions, but the correlation and mediation tables report N = 321, and the moderated regression reports N = 244 due to missing moderator data. The transition from 372 to 321 is not explained. This unexplained loss of 51 participants affects power, precision, and attrition/missingness interpretation.
issues.quote: This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.subcategory: attrition/exclusion arithmetic does not add up
issues.description: The manuscript reports 468 Time 1 respondents and 450 Time 4 respondents, then says only 16 people were excluded due to missing time points and 78 for poor data quality, yielding N = 372. However, 468 - 16 - 78 = 374, not 372; 450 - 78 = 372, implying the denominator changed to T4 completers. The exclusion accounting is internally inconsistent and obscures the true analytic sample derivation.
issues.quote: Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points) and whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality) were included in the final sample.

issues.subcategory: exclusion of nonresponders from later waves creates informative missingness risk
issues.description: Participants who missed a wave were not invited to later waves. This design converts intermittent missingness into permanent dropout and can induce attrition bias if missingness relates to workload, stress, incivility, fatigue, or shift schedules. The manuscript gives only a superficial comparison and does not use modern missing-data methods or sensitivity analyses.
issues.quote: Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys (i.e., a participant who did not complete T2 survey was not sent the link for the T3 or T4 surveys).

issues.subcategory: substantial missingness on moderator handled by listwise deletion
issues.description: The moderated regression sample is reduced from the stated final N = 372 or table N = 321 to N = 244 because of missing patient acuity data. This is a large reduction and may bias moderation estimates if missingness is related to unit type, acuity, stress, or respondent understanding. The manuscript describes missingness but does not report the number missing, missingness mechanisms, comparisons of included/excluded participants, or use imputation/FIML.
issues.quote: Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.subcategory: out-of-range moderator responses discarded without clear handling
issues.description: For patient acuity, 45% of missing values were due to values outside the expected range. This suggests many respondents misunderstood the measure or entered unusable responses. Treating these as missing without describing range checks, recoding rules, or whether invalidity was associated with respondent characteristics undermines confidence in the moderator analysis.
issues.quote: For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response).

issues.subcategory: single-item nonvalidated patient acuity measure
issues.description: Patient acuity is operationalized as a single self-reported percentage of patients considered “severe” based on heterogeneous departmental scales. This differs from objective acuity workload and may confound patient severity with subjective stress, mood, memory, caseload size, department, and respondents’ interpretation of “severe.” As a moderator, this measure may reflect generalized negative appraisal rather than acuity.
issues.quote: we measure the respondents’ perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were “severe.”

issues.subcategory: heterogeneous acuity scales not comparable
issues.description: The acuity item asks nurses across diverse specialties to use their own department’s acuity scale, with examples including ESI, CRIB, SOIS, and PRO tools. These scales measure different clinical constructs, populations, severity ranges, and scoring directions. Combining them as a percentage “severe” variable assumes cross-setting equivalence that is not demonstrated.
issues.quote: Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools

issues.subcategory: negative emotions construct limited to patient-directed emotions
issues.description: Negative emotions are measured as general frequency of frustration, irritability, anger, and resentment toward patients, not specifically emotions caused by experienced incivility. This creates ambiguity: negative emotions may stem from workload, patient suffering, staffing, moral distress, or trait affectivity. The mediator may not capture the proposed incivility-triggered emotional mechanism.
issues.quote: Participants were asked to rate “How often do you feel the following emotions towards patients” on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (Never) to 5 (Always).

issues.subcategory: experienced incivility source conflates patients and families
issues.description: The study labels the predictor as patient incivility, but the items combine patients with family members/friends. These are distinct sources with different power relations, contact patterns, and clinical implications. Enacted incivility similarly combines behavior toward patients and families. This conflation weakens construct precision and the interpretation that incivility is exchanged with “patients.”
issues.quote: how often have you been in a situation where any of your patients or patient family members/friends…

issues.subcategory: enacted incivility self-report may not validly capture actual behavior
issues.description: The enacted incivility measure asks nurses to admit mistreating patients/families in the past week. Because these behaviors are professionally and ethically sensitive, responses are likely affected by social desirability, self-awareness, and impression management. Without patient, coworker, supervisor, or observational corroboration, construct validity of enacted incivility is limited.
issues.quote: Participants were asked, “Thinking about your interactions with patients during the past week, how often have you…?”

issues.subcategory: convenience and network-based recruitment
issues.description: Recruitment relied on flyers at three local hospitals, personal networks, social media, forums, and self-selection by interested participants. This nonprobability sampling design can produce selection bias toward nurses with strong experiences or interest in incivility/wellbeing and limits inference to the broader nursing population.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies. First, we dropped off recruitment flyers... Second, we sent emails to nurses and other healthcare professionals in our personal networks... Finally, we posted study information and recruitment materials online via personal social network accounts

issues.subcategory: eligibility verification inadequate
issues.description: The authors relied on highlighting the nursing focus and directly asking participants if they met inclusion criteria. There is no verification of licensure, hospital employment, specialty, full-time status, or critical-care/high-stakes setting. Online recruitment through social media and networks increases risk of ineligible or duplicate participation.
issues.quote: To help ensure that the participants were from healthcare contexts, we highlighted the nursing focus in the recruitment and consent information and directly asked participants if they met the inclusion criteria.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent inclusion criteria full-time versus part-time
issues.description: Recruitment materials specified working full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting, but the final sample description says all participants were employed as nurses part- or full-time and worked more than one shift per week. This inconsistency affects the target population and interpretation of workload, acuity, and incivility exposure.
issues.quote: Information about inclusion criteria (working full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting as a nurse)

issues.subcategory: inconsistent final eligibility description
issues.description: The methods later state that all participants were currently employed as nurses part- or full-time, contradicting the earlier inclusion criterion that participants work full time. This could indicate protocol deviations or unclear eligibility screening.
issues.quote: All participants were currently employed as a nurse (part- or full-time), worked more than one shift a week, on average, and routinely worked with high severity/high-risk patients.

issues.subcategory: no clustering or site/unit effects modeled
issues.description: Participants were recruited from hospitals and likely nested within units or organizations, but the analyses appear to treat observations as independent. Shared unit climate, staffing, acuity norms, and hospital policies may induce clustering and confound associations. The manuscript does not report hospitals/units represented or intraclass correlations.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S.

issues.subcategory: missing details on recruitment yield and sample frame
issues.description: The manuscript states the full sampled population is unknown and does not report how many nurses saw recruitment materials, how many hospitals/units ultimately contributed participants, geographic distribution, response rate, or selection flow. Without this, representativeness and recruitment bias cannot be evaluated.
issues.quote: Although the full population size that was sampled from is unknown

issues.subcategory: overgeneralization from nurses to service employees/customers
issues.description: The paper frequently frames findings as applying to service employees and customers broadly, but the sample is mostly female nurses in high-stakes healthcare settings with specialized ethical, legal, emotional, and power dynamics. Generalizing to other service industries or ordinary customer interactions is only weakly supported.
issues.quote: Using a four-wave data collection of service employees within the healthcare industry, we examined how and why experiencing incivility from patients is related to future enactment of incivility towards patients.

issues.subcategory: patient-as-customer analogy limited
issues.description: The manuscript treats patients and families as customers, but patients differ from customers in vulnerability, dependence, suffering, involuntariness, legal/ethical obligations, and clinical acuity. This conceptual mapping may not support general claims about customer incivility without more careful boundary conditions.
issues.quote: We view the patient-nurse relationship as a specialized form of customer-employee relationship.

issues.subcategory: confusion between social learning theory and stressor-emotion model
issues.description: The introduction says the study utilizes social learning theory, then immediately describes the stressor-emotion model of CWB as the mechanism. Social learning theory concerns observational learning/modeling, whereas the hypotheses focus on stressor appraisal, negative emotion, and fatigue. The theoretical framing is inconsistent and social learning mechanisms are not measured or tested.
issues.quote: To understand how incivility experiences from customers may be impacting employee affect and behavior over time, we utilize social learning theory (Bandura, 1977). This model considers how individuals learn behaviors through observation and modeling of others' actions and their consequences, ultimately shaping counterproductive work behaviors (CWB), such as enacted incivility. Applied to enacted incivility, the general premise of the model suggests that enacted incivility occurs due to a sequence of events where environmental stressors at work lead to enacted incivility through appraisal, perceptions of the stressor, and negative emotions (Spector & Fox, 2005).

issues.subcategory: incorrect model name
issues.description: The manuscript refers to the “emotion-stressor model of CWB,” whereas the established model is the stressor-emotion model. This may be a typographical error, but it reflects conceptual imprecision in the theoretical framing.
issues.quote: Similarly, using the emotion-stressor model of CWB, Margulescu (2020) found that compassion fatigue was a predictor of CWB enactment.

issues.subcategory: compassion fatigue conceptualized as burnout but measured as composite without subdimensions
issues.description: The authors define compassion fatigue as including burnout and secondary trauma components but analyze it as a single 13-item score. They do not report whether the two-component structure holds in this sample or whether incivility relates differently to burnout versus secondary traumatic stress. Incivility from patients may plausibly predict burnout but not secondary trauma, so collapsing subdimensions may obscure construct validity.
issues.quote: Compassion fatigue consists of burnout and secondary trauma components, with employees experiencing compassion fatigue if they are experiencing either caregiving-related burnout or secondary trauma (or both of these simultaneously).

issues.subcategory: shortened scales without full validation in main sample
issues.description: The study uses shortened four-item versions of incivility scales and selected highest-loading items to reduce survey length. Although pilot part-whole correlations are reported, the main sample does not report item loadings, content coverage evidence, measurement invariance over waves, or whether shortened enacted and experienced scales remain distinct given similar item wording. This is a concern because shortened scales can narrow construct coverage.
issues.quote: For each scale, the highest loading items were chosen from reported factor analytic data to maintain a reasonable survey length and achieve internal consistency reliability

issues.subcategory: no preregistration or analysis plan reported
issues.description: The manuscript mentions a priori data-quality checks but does not report preregistration, a registered analysis plan, planned sample size/power analysis, planned exclusion rules in full, planned controls, or planned supplemental analyses. Given multiple waves, possible lag structures, controls, exclusions, and missing-data choices, undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom are substantial.
issues.quote: Responses were considered failed data quality checks if they had any of the following characteristics

issues.subcategory: no power analysis
issues.description: No a priori power analysis or precision justification is provided for the mediation or moderated mediation tests, especially the interaction and conditional indirect effects. The moderated analysis has only N = 244 after missingness, which may be underpowered for interaction and moderated mediation effects.
issues.quote: This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.subcategory: moderated mediation underpowered after missingness
issues.description: The test of moderation and moderated mediation uses N = 244, substantially smaller than the overall sample. Interaction effects and conditional indirect effects require larger samples, and the non-significant moderated mediation may reflect inadequate power. No power or sensitivity analysis is provided.
issues.quote: Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.subcategory: relative importance analysis interpretation questionable
issues.description: The supplemental relative importance analysis states that predictors accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility. These appear to be percentages of explained variance, not total variance, but the text says “of the variance.” With highly collinear predictors, relative importance metrics require careful interpretation. The analysis also differs from the main model coefficients, reporting compassion fatigue B = .23 rather than Table 2 B = .57, without explaining differences in scaling, samples, or controls.
issues.quote: The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.

issues.subcategory: relative importance coefficients conflict with Table 2
issues.description: The supplemental regression reports negative emotions and compassion fatigue both B = .23 when predicting enacted incivility, whereas Table 2 reports negative emotions B = .28 and compassion fatigue B = .57. The text says this analysis is based on predictors from the same stage, but the discrepancy is unexplained and undermines confidence in the reported models.
issues.quote: First, using the native lm() function in R (R Core Team, 2021), we regressed enacted incivility on predictors from this stage--experienced incivility (B = -.03, SE = .04, p = .40), negative emotions (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001), and compassion fatigue (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001).

issues.subcategory: confidence interval bracket typo
issues.description: The confidence interval for the index of moderated mediation is missing a closing bracket. Although minor, this is part of a broader pattern of imprecise statistical reporting.
issues.quote: the IMM was non-significant (B = .04, SE = .03, p = .15, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.11).

issues.subcategory: Table 3 formatting obscures coefficients
issues.description: Table 3 contains duplicated columns and misaligned headers, including repeated B columns and missing/ambiguous SE and t columns. This makes it difficult to determine the exact model estimates and evaluate the moderated regression results.
issues.quote: Variables | Customer Incivility (T2) | Customer Incivility (T2) | Customer Incivility (T2) | Customer Incivility (T2) | Negative Emotions (T3) | Negative Emotions (T3) | Negative Emotions (T3) | Negative Emotions (T3)

issues.subcategory: no explanation of time-lag choice specific to constructs
issues.description: The study uses weekly lags and cites prior studies, but does not justify why one week is the appropriate interval for negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility among nurses. Negative emotions may fluctuate within shifts, whereas compassion fatigue may develop over longer periods. Misspecified lags can bias longitudinal mediation tests.
issues.quote: Data were collected at four time points across four consecutive weeks, with each survey administered one week apart (i.e., interval contingent sampling).

issues.subcategory: chronic strain claims from four weeks of weekly retrospective data
issues.description: The manuscript frames incivility as chronic, cumulative, and prolonged, but the design covers only four weeks and measures past-week retrospective frequency. This limited window does not establish chronic exposure or accumulation, nor does the analysis model cumulative exposure or trajectories.
issues.quote: this cumulative strain experience may impact future enacted incivility. Here, we examine negative emotions and compassion fatigue as mechanisms

issues.subcategory: no modeling of repeated measures despite four-wave design
issues.description: Although each construct was measured at all four waves, the primary analyses appear to use selected single-wave variables rather than a longitudinal panel model, multilevel model, latent growth model, or cross-lagged model. This discards information, does not separate within-person from between-person effects, and undermines claims about processes unfolding over time.
issues.quote: We tested our hypotheses using data collected across four waves separated by one-week lags... The subsequent waves were included for hypothesis testing

issues.subcategory: between-person associations interpreted as within-person process
issues.description: The analyses appear to regress later variables on prior variables across individuals. Such models primarily test whether nurses who report higher incivility also report higher later emotions/fatigue/incivility, not whether increases within a nurse lead to subsequent increases. The discussion describes within-person temporal unfolding and accumulation, which is not established.
issues.quote: Our study suggests that the experienced-enacted incivility relationship unfolds over time and that experienced incivility can have lasting effects beyond the work week they are experienced in.

issues.subcategory: potential omitted confounders
issues.description: The models do not appear to control for key confounders such as trait negative affectivity, baseline mental health, job role/unit, shift type, patient load, staffing ratios, coworker/supervisor incivility, burnout history, sleep, tenure, or organizational climate. These factors could influence both experienced incivility perceptions and enacted incivility self-reports.
issues.quote: Our results suggest that employees experiencing high levels of incivility from patients are more likely to engage in future incivility behaviors

issues.subcategory: data quality exclusion criteria insufficiently specified
issues.description: Seventy-eight participants were excluded for poor data quality, mostly inconsistent demographics, but the manuscript does not describe the exact thresholds for “reasonably consistent” tenure, age, or gender responses, whether exclusions were blind to outcomes, or whether excluded participants differed on substantive variables. Such exclusions can materially affect results.
issues.quote: n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age

issues.subcategory: data quality exclusion categories do not sum to total
issues.description: The manuscript says 78 people were excluded for poor data quality, then lists n = 56 for inconsistent demographics and n = 1 for >50% missing, totaling 57, leaving 21 exclusions unexplained. This omission undermines the sample flow and replicability of exclusions.
issues.quote: whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality) ... (a) demographic information was not consistent ... (n = 56 people ...); or (b) missing values exceeded 50% of the questions (n = 1).

issues.subcategory: pilot sample for scale validation from MTurk nurses questionable
issues.description: The quantitative pilot used MTurk to recruit nurses in high-stakes settings. MTurk occupational samples may include misrepresentation, and no verification is described. Using this pilot to support shortened-scale validity and acuity item comprehension may be weak evidence for the target population.
issues.quote: The quantitative pilot consisted of n = 50 nurses who worked in high-stakes settings and were recruited from MTurk.

issues.subcategory: reliability over waves incomplete
issues.description: Cronbach’s alpha is shown for some variables on the diagonal in Table 1, but not for all waves of all scales, and single-item patient acuity has no reliability estimate. Given repeated measurement, scale adaptation, and shortened forms, reporting reliability and measurement invariance across all waves is needed.
issues.quote: Cronbach’s α presented on the diagonal.

issues.subcategory: correlation table uses customer incivility whereas text uses patient incivility
issues.description: The measures and hypotheses refer to patient incivility, while tables label the variable as customer incivility. Because the manuscript also includes patient families/friends, inconsistent labeling contributes to construct ambiguity.
issues.quote: T1 Customer Incivility

issues.subcategory: Table 1 significance notation questionable
issues.description: Table 1 notes that coefficients above |.20| are significant at p < .001 and marks some smaller correlations with *p < .05. However, with N = 321, correlations around .13 may be p < .05, but exact p-values and treatment of multiple correlations are not addressed. The large number of correlations increases familywise false-positive risk, and the table does not indicate whether pairwise or listwise N varies due to missingness.
issues.quote: Note. N = 321. Cronbach’s α presented on the diagonal. Coefficients above |.20| significant at p < .001. *p < .05

issues.subcategory: supplemental analyses not clearly prespecified
issues.description: The manuscript reports supplemental analyses of unhypothesized moderation and relative importance without stating whether these were planned. Exploratory analyses should be clearly labeled and interpreted cautiously, especially when they are used to support theoretical claims about compassion fatigue being a stronger driver.
issues.quote: Supplemental analyses. We conducted a series of supplemental analyses to 1) address unhypothesized moderation effects and 2) investigate the relationship between compassion fatigue and enacted incivility.

issues.subcategory: reverse causation not adequately tested
issues.description: Nurses who enact incivility may elicit negative reactions from patients/families, perceive more incivility, or experience more negative emotions and fatigue. The design includes multiple waves but does not report reciprocal or cross-lagged models testing enacted incivility as a predictor of later experienced incivility or emotions. This is particularly important given the “incivility begets incivility” framing.
issues.quote: experienced patient incivility is related to increased future enacted incivility towards patients indirectly through increased negative emotions and compassion fatigue

issues.subcategory: patient-family repeated relationship not measured
issues.description: The hypotheses assume generalized spillover across patients, but some nurses may interact with the same patients or families across weeks. The study does not measure whether incivility and enactment involve the same individuals, different individuals, or unit-level environments, limiting interpretation of the mechanism as spillover versus retaliation or ongoing dyadic conflict.
issues.quote: Third, another limitation to the longitudinal design of this study is the chance that an employee may continue an uncivil relationship with certain patients across various time points (i.e., via retribution pathways).

issues.subcategory: figures not provided with numerical details
issues.description: The manuscript refers to Figure 1 for measurement timing and Figure 2 for results, but the text provided does not include the figures’ substantive contents. Because the analytic timing is complex and inconsistently reported, missing figure details impede evaluation of the hypothesized and tested models.
issues.quote: see Figure 1 for information what measurement period each variable in the model was taken from

issues.subcategory: gender distribution limits generalization
issues.description: The sample is 96.64% female, higher than the nursing workforce estimate cited by the authors. Although nursing is female-dominated, such imbalance limits ability to generalize to male nurses or examine gendered power dynamics in incivility experiences and enactment.
issues.quote: The majority of respondents were female (96.64%)

issues.subcategory: clinical setting composition not reported
issues.description: The study targets high-stakes or critical-care nurses but does not report the distribution across emergency departments, ICUs, operating rooms, pediatrics/neonatal units, etc. These contexts differ greatly in patient acuity scales, family involvement, incivility risk, and shift structure. Without this information, replicability and boundary conditions are unclear.
issues.quote: particularly those working in high-stakes or critical care settings

issues.subcategory: compensation and repeated-survey incentives may affect data quality
issues.description: Participants received small gift cards for each weekly survey. While common, the study had substantial data-quality exclusions and online recruitment, yet does not report safeguards against duplicate entries, bots, inattentive responding beyond demographic consistency, or professional misrepresentation.
issues.quote: Participants received a $5 gift card for each survey they completed (with a possible $20 total earned).

issues.subcategory: moderated mediation claim inconsistent with nonsignificant conditional indirect effects
issues.description: The discussion emphasizes that patient acuity exacerbates the process leading to behavior, but supplemental moderated mediation showed nonsignificant conditional indirect effects and nonsignificant IMM. Thus, acuity moderated only the first-stage relationship with negative emotions, not the indirect relationship to enacted incivility. Statements implying the entire cascade to behavior is exacerbated overstate the statistical findings.
issues.quote: In addition, these processes can be exacerbated when nurses are also perceiving  high patient care-related demands, suggesting that nurses are at increased risk of the negative emotional processes and behaviors when they are simultaneously experiencing interpersonal ... and task-related ... stressors.

issues.subcategory: abstract overstates moderated pathway
issues.description: The abstract says patient acuity can exacerbate detrimental relationships and then describes indirect effects to enacted incivility, but the reported moderated mediation was nonsignificant. This may mislead readers into thinking acuity moderated the full indirect effect.
issues.quote: experienced patient incivility is positively related to negative emotions and to compassion fatigue, and that perceived patient acuity can exacerbate these detrimental relationships. Lastly, experienced patient incivility is related to increased future enacted incivility towards patients indirectly through increased negative emotions and compassion fatigue.

issues.subcategory: model estimation details insufficient
issues.description: The manuscript says analyses used MPlus model constraints and Monte Carlo simulations but does not fully specify estimator for structural models, handling of nonnormal ordinal Likert outcomes, centering of interaction terms, treatment of missing data, whether robust SEs were used, or whether variables were manifest composites or latent variables. These details are necessary for replication.

issues.subcategory: Likert means treated as continuous without discussion
issues.description: All key variables are based on 5-point frequency Likert scales, with many potentially skewed socially undesirable behaviors. The analyses use linear regression/path models without reporting distributions, skewness, floor/ceiling effects, or robustness checks. Enacted incivility especially may be nonnormal and ordinal.
issues.quote: Responses were rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (Never) to 5 (Always).

issues.subcategory: enacted incivility mean implausibly high
issues.description: The reported mean for enacted incivility is high (T4 M = 2.77 on a 1–5 Never–Always scale), implying nurses often admit uncivil behavior toward patients/families. Given the social undesirability of these behaviors and the professional context, this raises questions about item interpretation, sample validity, or response quality. The manuscript does not discuss this surprising prevalence.
issues.quote: T4 Enacted Incivility | 2.77 | 1.21

issues.subcategory: experienced and enacted incivility items are mirror-worded
issues.description: Experienced and enacted incivility use very similar item wording with only source/target reversed. This can inflate correlations through item wording and response consistency, especially in the same self-report survey, and may not adequately distinguish being mistreated from mistreating others.
issues.quote: The item content for these four items was similar to the four items used in the customer incivility scale, with changes to the instructions that prompted participants to respond about how they behaved towards their patients

issues.subcategory: no ethics/IRB information reported
issues.description: The study surveys nurses about potentially unethical behavior toward patients and workplace experiences, yet no institutional review board approval, consent details, confidentiality protections beyond general assurance, or data security procedures are reported. This is important for ethical evaluation and participant candor.
issues.quote: Participants initiated the contact and study procedures by clicking on the study link or QR code that was listed in recruitment materials

issues.subcategory: CFA factor count inconsistent with five constructs
issues.description: The manuscript reports a four-factor CFA, but the study includes experienced incivility, negative emotions, compassion fatigue, enacted incivility, and patient acuity. Patient acuity may be single-item and excluded, but this exclusion is not clearly explained. If patient acuity is part of the model, measurement validity for it is not assessed; if excluded, the “four-factor” model does not cover all substantive constructs.
issues.quote: First, we assessed our hypothesized four-factor model absent of the temporal control measures.

issues.subcategory: hypothesis 2 wording and analysis mismatch
issues.description: Hypothesis 2 predicts an indirect relationship between experienced incivility and compassion fatigue through negative emotions. However, the results also report a significant direct effect and the discussion calls the model “partial mediation.” The analytic model appears to include direct paths, but the hypothesis text does not specify partial versus full mediation or whether direct effects were expected.
issues.quote: Of note, the direct relationship between experienced patient incivility and compassion fatigue was also significant (B = .13, SE = .03, p < .001).

issues.subcategory: patient acuity as moderator lacks appraisal measurement
issues.description: The theoretical rationale relies on stress appraisal, arguing acuity changes whether incivility is appraised as stressful, but no appraisal or threat perception measure is included. Patient acuity is therefore only a proxy for a proposed appraisal process, leaving the theoretical mechanism untested.
issues.quote: Part of the stressor-emotion model of CWB relies on the stressor being appraised and perceived as stressful.

issues.subcategory: work hours control may be collider or suppressor without rationale
issues.description: Work hours are included as controls in some models and show large negative correlations with key variables, which is counterintuitive. The manuscript does not justify work hours as a confounder, explain why it is included in some equations but not others, or assess whether controlling for it induces bias or suppression.

issues.subcategory: negative relationship between work hours and incivility/fatigue unexplained
issues.description: Table 1 shows work hours negatively correlated around -.35 to -.44 with incivility, negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility. This is surprising and may indicate coding errors, sample artifacts, part-time/full-time inconsistencies, or confounding by leave/sick time. The manuscript does not discuss these patterns.
issues.quote: T3 Negative Emotions ... -.44 ... T4 Compassion Fatigue ... -.39 ... T4 Enacted Incivility ... -.40

issues.subcategory: no descriptive information on missing acuity denominator
issues.description: Patient acuity is measured as percentage of severe patients, but the number of patients seen is not reported. A percentage based on 2 patients is not comparable to a percentage based on 20 patients, and measurement error will vary substantially. The authors acknowledge this limitation only in discussion, but the analysis does not account for it.
issues.quote: we did not ask them to report on the specific assessment used, number of patients seen in that week, or the number of patients that were actually classified as severe within their assessment tool.

issues.subcategory: no blinding or objective outcome safeguards
issues.description: Although blinding is less applicable in survey studies, respondents were aware of their own experiences and outcomes and may infer the study purpose from repeated incivility/emotion/fatigue questions. No steps beyond confidentiality are described to reduce demand characteristics or consistency motifs.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks.

issues.subcategory: survey timing relative to shifts unclear
issues.description: The surveys ask about the past week, but the timing relative to work shifts, days off, night shifts, and recent adverse events is not specified. For nurses, whether a survey was completed immediately after a difficult shift versus after days off could strongly affect recall and affective reports.
issues.quote: For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week.

issues.subcategory: compassion fatigue over one-week recall may not match construct
issues.description: Compassion fatigue is usually a more enduring syndrome involving burnout and secondary traumatic stress. Measuring it weekly with items like losing sleep over a patient’s traumatic experiences may capture transient distress or mood rather than compassion fatigue as conceptualized. The manuscript does not validate weekly sensitivity of the scale.
issues.quote: For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week.

issues.subcategory: US-only sample but broad service-sector implications
issues.description: The study recruits from the U.S. and references U.S. nursing employment, yet implications are framed broadly for service industries. Healthcare systems, nurse roles, patient norms, staffing, and incivility norms vary by country, limiting international generalizability.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S.

issues.subcategory: incivility versus verbal aggression boundary blurred
issues.description: The paper draws on customer verbal aggression literature and high-stakes healthcare mistreatment, but incivility is defined as low-intensity and ambiguous intent. Some patient/family behaviors in clinical crises may be high-intensity aggression or distress-related challenge rather than incivility. The study does not distinguish incivility from aggression, justified complaints, or safety-related patient concerns.

issues.subcategory: item may capture legitimate patient advocacy rather than incivility
issues.description: The experienced incivility item “Doubted your judgment” may in healthcare reflect legitimate patient/family concern, shared decision-making, advocacy, or requests for clarification, not necessarily rude or uncivil behavior. This threatens construct validity in the patient-care context.
issues.quote: “Doubted your judgment on a matter over which you had responsibility,”

issues.subcategory: enacted item may capture clinical skepticism rather than incivility
issues.description: The enacted item “Doubted one or more patient’s/patient family members’ judgment” may be part of clinical assessment or safety-related correction rather than uncivil behavior. Without context, this item may not validly reflect low-intensity deviance toward patients.

issues.subcategory: ordinal CFA estimator not matched to subsequent manifest regressions
issues.description: The CFA uses WLSMV at item level, appropriate for ordinal items, but the structural mediation analyses appear to use manifest scale scores in regression/path analysis with normal-theory assumptions. The manuscript does not justify this shift or report robustness to ordinal/non-normal estimation.

issues.subcategory: no model fit for structural models
issues.description: For the mediation and moderated mediation models, no SEM/path model fit indices are reported, despite use of MPlus and model constraints. issues.subcategory: confidence intervals not consistently reported for all key estimates
issues.description: CIs are provided for some indirect effects and simple slopes but not for key direct paths, interaction estimates, R², or relative importance metrics. Given mediation and moderation uncertainty, comprehensive intervals would improve evaluation.
issues.quote: experienced patient incivility was positively related to negative emotions toward patients (B = .26, SE = .06, p < .001).

issues.subcategory: retention rates misleading after excluding missed-wave participants
issues.description: Retention is reported as 98% between waves, but participants who missed a wave were not invited subsequently, and analytic sample exclusions substantially reduce the sample. Reporting only conditional retention rates may obscure cumulative attrition and exclusion impact.

issues.subcategory: attrition comparison inadequate
